skills.name: Practical: observing plant and animal cells under the microscope

note.text:
Onion epidermis (plant cells): peel a thin layer from the inside of an onion scale, lay it flat in a drop of water or iodine solution on a slide, lower a cover slip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, observe at low then high power.
Cheek cells (animal cells): gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a clean spatula, smear on a slide, add a drop of methylene blue, cover and observe.
Stains make parts visible: iodine stains the nucleus and starch; methylene blue stains the nucleus.
Biological drawings: pencil, clear single lines, no shading, label lines ruled and not crossing, state the magnification.
Total magnification = eyepiece × objective.

sections.heading: Preparing an onion slide
sections.text:
• Peel a thin, almost transparent layer (epidermis) from the inside of an onion scale with forceps.
• Lay it flat in a drop of iodine solution on a clean slide.
• Lower a cover slip at an angle, using a mounted needle, so no air bubbles are trapped.
• Observe under low power first, then high power.
You will see a brick-like pattern of cells, each with a cell wall and a dark nucleus.

sections.heading: Preparing cheek cells
sections.text:
• Gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a clean spatula (or the flat end of a clean toothpick).
• Smear the scrapings on a slide, add a drop of methylene blue and cover.
• Throw used spatulas into disinfectant.
The cells are irregular in shape, with a blue nucleus and no cell wall.

sections.heading: Microscope and drawings
sections.text:
Total magnification = eyepiece × objective: ×{10} and ×{40} give ×{400}.
Draw what you see, not what you expect: sharp pencil, clear single lines, no shading, ruled label lines that do not cross, a title and the magnification.
Then you can work out real sizes: real size = drawing size ÷ magnification.

key_words.meaning: a thin outer layer of cells
a dye that makes cell parts visible
a thin square of glass placed over the specimen

examples: Onion: iodine stain, cell wall visible
Cheek: methylene blue, no cell wall

mistake.why: The two lenses multiply the magnification.

worked_example.problem: A student uses a ×{e} eyepiece and a ×{o} objective lens. What is the total magnification?

cards.idea: Stains make cell parts easier to see.
example: Iodine for onion cells; methylene blue for cheek cells.

cards.idea: Lower the cover slip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.
example: Air bubbles look like black-edged circles.

questions.prompt: What is the total magnification with a ×{e} eyepiece and a ×{o} objective?

misconceptions.explain: Multiply the two magnifications, do not add them.

pick.q: Which stain is used for onion epidermis cells?
e: Methylene blue is usually used for cheek cells.
Ink is not a laboratory stain.
pick.y: Iodine stains the nucleus and any starch.

pick.q: Why is a stain added to cheek cells?
pick.r: To make the nucleus and other parts visible
pick.y: Cells are almost transparent without stain.

pick.q: Which structure can be seen in onion cells but not in cheek cells?
pick.y: Plant cells have a cellulose wall.

pick.q: Which is a rule for biological drawings?
pick.r: Use a sharp pencil and clear single lines without shading
w: Use a pen and colour the drawing
Draw label lines with arrow heads that cross
e: Label lines are ruled, without arrows, and must not cross.
pick.y: Clear, accurate pencil outlines are easiest to read.
The title and magnification tell the reader what and how big.

pick.q: You see black-edged circles on your slide. What are they most likely to be?
e: Nuclei are inside cells and stain.
pick.y: Lowering the cover slip carelessly traps air.

questions.prompt: Under ×{m} total magnification, an onion cell appears {img} mm long in your drawing. What is its real length (µm)?

misconceptions.explain: That is in mm; × {1000} for µm.
